694.title: Sulayman's du'a
694.hook: inspire me to be grateful, and to do good that pleases You (27:19)
694.howItsDone: Some Muslims say the du'a of 27:19, rabbi awzi'ni an ashkura ni'mataka, in moments of success or gratitude; the similar words of 46:15 are also taught as a du'a for parents and children.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zakariyya in the sanctuary, and your line: don't leave me alone. Did your message reach someone who needed it? Today, a king with everything, stopped in his tracks by an ant. Day six hundred ninety-four.

An army on the march: people, jinn and birds, the Qur'an says, all in their ranks, and at the front a king, Sulayman, the one the Bible calls Solomon. They come to a valley full of ants. And one ant calls out to the others: get into your homes, or Sulayman and his soldiers will crush you without even noticing. Surah twenty-seven says Sulayman heard her. He had been taught the speech of birds, the surah says, and here he understands an ant. And the king at the head of that army stops, and smiles.
screen: `AN ARMY IN THE VALLEY OF THE ANTS.`

segments.voice: What he does next is surah twenty-seven, verse nineteen. He smiled, laughing at her words, and prayed. In Pickthall's translation: "My Lord, arouse me to be thankful for Thy favour wherewith Thou hast favoured me and my parents, and to do good that shall be pleasing unto Thee." The word Pickthall renders arouse me is awzi'ni. Translators give it as inspire me, or keep me devoted, or urge me on. The point is the same: Sulayman doesn't trust himself to stay grateful on his own. He asks to be kept at it. Count what he has. A kingdom, an army, the speech of birds. And the moment that gift shows him something, a tiny creature worried about her family, his first reaction isn't pride. It's thanks, and a request for help to keep thanking. Notice too who he includes: me and my parents. The gift that let him hear an ant didn't start with him. Later in the same surah, when a throne is brought to him in the blink of an eye, he says, in effect, this is from my Lord's bounty, to test me whether I give thanks or turn ungrateful. So for Sulayman, a skill is also a question. One more detail: nearly the same words come back in surah forty-six, in the mouth of an ordinary person who reaches forty years old. The king's prayer turns out to be a prayer for anyone who has been given anything.
screen: `AWZI'NI: KEEP ME AT IT, INSPIRE ME.`

segments.voice: The practice: give thanks for one skill. Sit, and breathe. Pick one thing you can do: cook a dish without a recipe, calm a crying baby, fix a sink, make a stranger laugh, tie a knot that holds. Now trace it back. Who taught you, or who gave you the time to learn it? A parent, a teacher, a coworker who was patient once. If you pray, you can thank Allah for the skill and for the people behind it, in your own words or with Sulayman's. If you don't, simply hold the skill and the people with it, gratefully. The bell holds the time.
Sulayman's du'a. A king who heard an ant, smiled, and asked to be kept grateful, for himself and for his parents, and to do good that pleases Allah. Today's word.
Your line: inspire me to be grateful. Today, when someone praises something you do well, pass the praise along: name one person who taught you. Day six hundred ninety-four.

695.title: The believers' du'a
695.hook: our Lord, don't let our hearts swerve, and give us mercy from You (3:8)
695.tomorrow: Year two close: the book read through
695.howItsDone: Some Muslims say 3:8, rabbana la tuzigh qulubana, after the daily prayers or in personal du'a, alongside the Prophet's own prayer, ya muqallib al-qulub, thabbit qalbi 'ala dinik.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sulayman and the ant, and your line: inspire me to be grateful. Did you pass some praise along to the person who taught you? Today, the last du'a of this run, and the first spoken not by a prophet but by a whole group of believers. Day six hundred ninety-five.

Umm Salamah, one of the wives of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, noticed something. A prayer he said more than any other, she reported, was this: O turner of hearts, keep my heart firm on Your religion. She asked him why that one, so often. He answered, in the hadith recorded by al-Tirmidhi, that every human heart lies between two of the fingers of Allah, and He turns it as He wills. And this was the Prophet himself, asking again and again for his own heart to be kept.

The Qur'an puts a request very like it in the mouths of a whole group. Surah three, verse seven, talks about the book itself: some verses are clear and plain, others are open to more than one reading. Some people chase the unclear ones to stir up trouble, it says. But those firmly grounded in knowledge say: we believe in it, it is all from our Lord. And then, verse eight, in Pickthall's translation: "Our Lord! Cause not our hearts to stray after Thou hast guided us, and bestow upon us mercy from Thy Presence. Lo! Thou, only Thou, art the Bestower." Look at who is praying. Not beginners. The people the verse calls firm in knowledge, the ones who have studied the hard parts. And look at the phrase after Thou hast guided us. This isn't a prayer to find the way. It's a prayer not to lose it. Guidance, in this verse, is not a trophy you keep on a shelf. It can slip. And the Prophet's own words make the fit audible: muqallib al-qulub, turner of hearts. Qalb, heart, and the verb to turn share their letters, as if a heart is the thing that turns. So those who know the hard parts ask, like the Prophet did, to be kept. This whole week has been prophets' du'as: Adam, Ibrahim, Musa, Ayyub, Yunus, Zakariyya, Sulayman. Today's belongs to everyone who has been guided at all.
screen: `THE FIRMLY GROUNDED SAY: ALL FROM OUR LORD.`
`DON'T LET OUR HEARTS STRAY, AFTER GUIDANCE.`

segments.voice: The practice: say it after prayer. Sit, and find your heartbeat if you can, steady, without your help. If you pray, you can say the believers' words, in Arabic if you know them, or in English: our Lord, don't let our hearts swerve after You have guided us, and give us mercy from You. Some Muslims say it after the daily prayer. If you don't pray, think of one thing you hold dear that you'd hate to drift from, and simply hold it while the heart keeps time. The bell holds the time.

The believers' du'a. Our Lord, don't let our hearts swerve after guidance, and give us mercy from You. Said by those firm in knowledge, and close to the prayer the Prophet said most often. Today's word.
Your line: keep my heart. Today, pick one good habit you already have and give it a small guard: set the reminder, lay out the mat, put the book where you'll see it. Day six hundred ninety-five.

696.title: Year two close: the book read through
696.hook: from the Opening to the thirtieth part, the whole Qur'an has now been heard once
696.howItsDone: Many Muslims complete a reading of the whole Qur'an, a khatm, especially during Ramadan, often closing with a gathering and du'a, and in many communities a new reading begins at once with the Fatiha and the opening of al-Baqarah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the believers' du'a, and your line: keep my heart. Did you put a small guard around one good habit? Today, the last day of year two, and a whole book behind you. Day six hundred ninety-six.

On the first day of this year, your line was: from the opening, onward. You were asked to choose a daily reading time. Since then this path has walked from surah one, the Fatiha, through the Cow and the Family of Imran, past Yusuf and Maryam and the Cave, through the Ant and the Stories, all the way to surah seventy-seven. Year one had already carried the last part, the thirtieth, from seventy-eight to the end. Put the two years together, and something has happened quietly.

Every one of the hundred and fourteen surahs has now been heard on this path at least once. Let's be honest about what that means. The short surahs came whole. The long ones came by theme, a passage and an idea at a time, not every verse read aloud. So this is a first hearing, not a full recitation. But it has a shape Muslims know well. Finishing the Qur'an from beginning to end is called a khatm, a sealing or completing, and it has a long history. A hadith in al-Bukhari says the angel Jibril went over the Qur'an with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ once every Ramadan, and twice in the year he died. Many Muslims aim for a khatm each Ramadan; some families and mosques gather to hear its final surahs together and make du'a. And in many communities, the moment one reading ends, the next one begins: back to the Fatiha, and the first lines of the Cow. The book has no last page, only a place where you turn around. The year was built in five blocks: the Opening and the long Medinan surahs; prophets, parables and light; a holy-days interlude; the middle of the book; and then the run toward the thirtieth part. The last month gathered it all: the prophets named, the women remembered, justice, mercy, the earth, and this past week, the prophets' own du'as. Pickthall's translation of the Fatiha opens: "In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful. Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds." That is where the reading began. It is also where the next one starts.
screen: `A FIRST HEARING, NOT A FULL RECITATION.`

segments.voice: The practice: the Fatiha, and your carried verse. Sit, and let your breath slow. If you pray, recite the Fatiha, in Arabic if you know it, or hear its meaning in English, line by line. Then bring back one verse from this year that stayed with you. Maybe a healing and a mercy. Maybe I was wrong. Maybe no compulsion. Say it once, or simply hold it. If you don't pray, just let one line from the year come back to you, and notice why it was that one that stayed. The bell holds the time.
Year two close. From the Fatiha to surah seventy-seven, joined to last year's thirtieth part: every surah, heard once. A khatm, and a door back to the beginning. Today's word.

Your line: the whole book, heard once. Today, write down the one verse you're carrying out of this year, and put it where next year will find it. Tomorrow, year three: the people who carried this book. Day six hundred ninety-six.

697.title: The long story
697.hook: a year of people: the Prophet ﷺ, those who walked beside him, and those who came after
697.howItsDone: Sirah books and mosque classes teach the life of the Prophet ﷺ alongside the Qur'an, and Muslims pray, in words from surah fifty-nine, for forgiveness for those who came before them in faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed year two. Your line was: the whole book, heard once. Did you write down the verse you're carrying, and where did you put it so this year would find it? Day six hundred ninety-seven.

A book doesn't walk from one century to the next on its own. Someone memorized it. Someone recited it at dawn to a child who was half asleep. Someone copied it, taught it, argued over it, carried it on a camel or in a coat pocket. For two years this path has listened to the Qur'an itself, surah by surah. This year turns around and looks at the people standing next to it: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, the ones who walked beside him, and the long line who came after. Today's word is the shape of that year.
screen: `A BOOK DOESN'T WALK ON ITS OWN.` → `TWO YEARS OF THE TEXT.` → `NOW, THE PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Muslims have a word for the story of the Prophet's life: sirah. One of the early lives that comes down to us was put together by Ibn Ishaq, and it reaches us largely through a later editor, Ibn Hisham. When this year says the sirah tells, that is the kind of book it means. Then there are the companions, the sahabah. The Qur'an itself remembers one of them without giving his name. In surah nine it describes the Prophet hiding in a cave on his escape from Mecca, and Pickthall's translation reads: "the second of two; when they two were in the cave, when he said unto his comrade: Grieve not. Lo! Allah is with us." Commentators identify that comrade as Abu Bakr. A whole friendship, inside one verse. And then the ones after. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet is reported to say that the best people are his own generation, then those who follow them, then those who follow them. Link after link. A hadith comes with its isnad, the chain of names attached to it: this one heard it from that one, who heard it from another. Every saying arrives holding someone's hand. So here is the rule this year will keep. The Qur'an and the major hadith collections come first. The sirah adds color and detail, and where a story is told only by later writers, or told different ways, this path will say so out loud. And the people will be people: brave, frightened, generous, sometimes wrong. The Qur'an calls the Messenger a good example. The people around him show what following it looked like up close: a frightened friend in a cave, being told not to grieve.
screen: `SIRAH: THE STORY OF A LIFE.` · `THE SECOND OF TWO, IN THE CAVE.` · `HIS GENERATION, THEN THE NEXT.` · `QUR'AN FIRST, THEN THE SIRAH.` · then, large: `GRIEVE NOT. LO! ALLAH IS WITH US.`

segments.voice: The practice: one person from history you admire. Settle, and let your breathing slow. Bring to mind someone who lived before you, famous or not: a scholar, a great-grandmother, a teacher whose name is on a building, a companion whose story you half remember. Hold their face, or what you imagine of it. Then ask what they carried that reached you. A skill, a book, a kind of courage, a habit at the dinner table. If you pray, you can ask Allah's mercy for them. If you don't, simply stay with them, and let yourself notice that it came this far because they carried it. The bell holds the time.
The long story. A year of people: the Prophet ﷺ, his companions, and those who came after, each one handing it to the next. Today's word.

Your line: people carried it. Today, say the name of the person you admire out loud to someone, and tell them one thing that person carried. Tomorrow, the land where the story starts. Day six hundred ninety-seven.

698.title: The peninsula
698.hook: desert, oases, trade routes, and a people who prized poetry and hospitality
698.carry: a land of wells and words
698.howItsDone: Mosque classes and sirah books often begin the Prophet's story with the land of Arabia before Islam: Mecca's dry valley, its trade, and the customs of hospitality and poetry the Qur'an's first listeners knew.

segments.voice: Yesterday the long story began, and your line was: people carried it. Whose name did you say out loud, and what had they carried to you? Day six hundred ninety-eight.

Sand ridges, for days. Then, low on the horizon, a smudge of green: date palms around a well. A line of camels turns toward it, and everyone in the caravan already knows that well's name, who holds it, and what it costs to drink there. This is where the long story starts. Before a single verse came down, before the Prophet ﷺ was born, there was this land of distances, water, and words. Today we stand in it for a while.
screen: `SAND, FOR DAYS.` → `A SMUDGE OF GREEN.` → `WHERE THE STORY STARTS.`

segments.voice: Arabic calls the place jazirat al-'arab, the island of the Arabs, since the word jazirah can mean island or peninsula. The Qur'an speaks to people who knew this land in their bodies. When Ibrahim leaves his family near the House, his prayer in surah fourteen calls the place, in Pickthall's words, "an uncultivable valley near unto Thy holy House." No crops. Tradition places Mecca in that valley. So how did people live there? Trade. Surah one hundred six, named for the tribe of Quraysh, speaks of their caravans setting out in winter and in summer, and asks them to worship the Lord of this House, who fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear. Caravans, food, safety: a desert town's living, in a few short lines. Not all of the land was empty, though. There were oases, with wells and palm groves, and towns grew up around them. One of them the Qur'an calls Yathrib, the town that would later be known as Medina. Between the oases ran the routes, and along the routes, tradition remembers two things held in honor. The first was hospitality. Where a traveler without water could die, taking in a guest was not a nicety. Stories are still told of Hatim of the tribe of Tayy, remembered as a byword for giving. The second was words. Tradition remembers poems memorized and recited at fairs and around fires. A good line could make a tribe proud. A sharp one could wound. Hold those two together, because the Qur'an arrives in exactly this world. When it speaks of rain from the sky bringing dead land back to life, its first listeners knew what dead land looked like. And when it challenged them to bring a surah like it, it was speaking to listeners who knew what language could do.
screen: `AN UNCULTIVABLE VALLEY.` · `CARAVANS IN WINTER AND SUMMER.` · `OASES, AND A TOWN CALLED YATHRIB.` · `HOSPITALITY AND POETRY.` · then, large: `NEAR UNTO THY HOLY HOUSE.`

segments.voice: The practice: a vast, empty place. Sit comfortably, and close your eyes if you like. See a wide open land: sand, or sea, or snow, whatever empty looks like to you. No roads. No signal. Let the space grow a little with each breath out. Then notice what you would long for there: water, shade, a voice, another person. Those were the things this land made precious. If you pray, you can thank Allah for one of them you have today. If you don't, simply notice which one you would miss first. The bell holds the time.
The peninsula. Arabia before the message: desert and oases, caravans and wells, hospitality and poetry. Today's word.
Your line: a land of wells and words. Today, when you drink a glass of water, take one sip slowly, and remember a valley with no crops. Tomorrow, the tribes. Day six hundred ninety-eight.

699.title: The tribes
699.hook: life was held together by tribe and clan, for protection and for honor
699.howItsDone: Qur'an 49:13 is recited in sermons and classes on family, race and belonging, and the hadith about helping an oppressor by stopping him is taught alongside it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the peninsula. Your line was: a land of wells and words. Did you take that one slow sip of water, and remember a valley with no crops? Day six hundred ninety-nine.

Who are your people? In Mecca before Islam, the answer to that question could decide whether you lived. Ask a man his name and he would give you a chain: son of this one, of that clan, of that tribe. There was no police force and no state. Your clan was your protection. Harm one of its members and the whole clan answered. Lose your clan and you stood alone in the open, with nobody to answer for you. Today's word is the thing that held that world together.
screen: `WHO ARE YOUR PEOPLE?` → `NO POLICE, NO STATE.` → `YOUR CLAN WAS YOUR SHIELD.`

segments.voice: The word is qabilah: a tribe. As the sirah describes it, a tribe was made of clans, and clans of families, nested like rooms in a house. In Mecca the tribe was Quraysh, and among its clans was Banu Hashim, the clan the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ would be born into. Belonging gave you honor, a name to stand behind, and above all protection. The custom of blood vengeance meant an attack on one person was an attack on the clan, and that threat kept people safe. It also kept feuds burning. That protective side matters later in this story: the sirah tells how the Prophet's uncle Abu Talib, of the same clan, sheltered him when others turned hostile. But tribal loyalty could also mean standing by your own whether they were right or wrong. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet says: help your brother, whether he is an oppressor or oppressed. The companions were puzzled. Helping the oppressed, yes. But how do you help an oppressor? By stopping him from oppressing, he answered. Some readers hear in the first half an echo of an old desert saying, turned inside out by the second. Loyalty stays. Its job changes. And then the Qur'an. Surah forty-nine uses this very word, in the plural. Pickthall translates: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." Tribes are not erased. They are given a purpose: knowing one another. And the verse goes on, in Pickthall's words: "Lo! the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct." In a world that measured honor by lineage, that turned the ladder sideways. Your line still names you. It no longer ranks you.
screen: `QABILAH: TRIBE, CLAN, FAMILY.` · `THE CLAN WAS YOUR PROTECTION.` · `HELP YOUR BROTHER, OPPRESSOR OR OPPRESSED.` · `TRIBES, THAT YE MAY KNOW ONE ANOTHER.` · then, large: `THE NOBLEST OF YOU IS THE BEST IN CONDUCT.`

segments.voice: The practice: thank your own people. Sit, and let your breath settle. Bring to mind your people: family by blood, or the ones you chose, or a community that took you in. Let a few faces come. Who stood behind you when you were in trouble? Who gave you a name to stand on? Let one of them come close, and stay with them for a while. If you pray, you can thank Allah for them and ask good for them. If you don't, just say thank you silently, as if they could hear it. The bell holds the time.
Qabilah. A tribe: clans and families bound together for protection and honor. Surah forty-nine uses its plural: tribes, that you may know one another. Today's word.
Your line: belonging protected you. Today, send one message to someone among your own people, just to say they're on your mind. Tomorrow, poets at the fair. Day six hundred ninety-nine.

700.title: Poets at the fair
700.hook: at the fairs of 'Ukaz poets competed, and the best odes were honored
700.howItsDone: Classical Arabic poetry from before Islam is still studied by Muslims and students of Arabic, partly to understand the language the Qur'an's first listeners knew; the Qur'an itself is recited, not sung as poetry.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tribes. The word was qabilah, and your line was: belonging protected you. Who did you send that message to? Day seven hundred.

Dust, tents, the smell of leather and spice. Traders have come from across the peninsula to a market called 'Ukaz. But one crowd isn't gathered around the goods. It's gathered around a man standing up to speak. He opens his mouth and a long poem comes out, measured and rhymed, line after line landing on the same sound. When he finishes, people repeat his best lines to each other. By the time the caravans leave, those lines will travel farther than any bale of cloth. Today: poets at the fair.
screen: `A MARKET CALLED 'UKAZ.` → `A CROWD AROUND A SPEAKER.` → `LINES THAT TRAVEL.`

segments.voice: Ibn Abbas, a young cousin of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, names 'Ukaz in Sahih al-Bukhari as one of the markets of the days before Islam. Later writers remember it as a place where poets performed and were judged. The Arabic word for poet is sha'ir. Poems that come down from that time praised a tribe's courage, mourned the dead, described a camel, or lingered over an abandoned campsite where a beloved once lived. Tradition says a great poem could make a tribe famous, and a mocking one could shame it. Later writers gathered a set of odes called the Mu'allaqat, the hung ones, and a story people tell says they were hung on the Ka'ba. That story is disputed, and the name's first meaning is uncertain. Now bring the long story back in. When the Qur'an came, it came to listeners who knew good language the way some people know good bread. Some in Mecca called the Prophet a poet; surah fifty-two quotes them saying so. The Qur'an answers them directly. Surah thirty-six says Allah did not teach him poetry, and that it does not befit him. Surah sixty-nine says this is not the speech of a poet. That isn't the Qur'an calling poetry worthless. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet says that some poetry is wisdom. It is the Qur'an saying: this is something else. And the people best placed to hear the difference were the ones who had stood in the crowd at 'Ukaz, and knew exactly what a poem sounded like.
screen: `'UKAZ: A MARKET BEFORE ISLAM.` · `SHA'IR: POET.` · `THE HUNG ODES, AND A DISPUTED STORY.` · `NOT THE SPEECH OF A POET.` · then, large: `SOME POETRY IS WISDOM.`

segments.voice: The practice: read a line of poetry aloud. Find one line: a verse a grandparent used to quote, a line from school, a lyric you love, a few words of the Qur'an if you know them. Say it aloud, slowly, once. Then say it again, softer. Listen to the sound: where it rises, where it lands, which word carries the weight. Then sit in the quiet after it for the rest of the time. If you pray, you can thank Allah for the gift of speech. If you don't, simply notice what a few words just did to the room. The bell holds the time.
Poets at the fair. At 'Ukaz and markets like it, poets recited and were judged, and a good line could travel farther than any caravan. Today's word.
Your line: words had power. Today, choose one sentence you say to someone, and give it the care a poet at the fair would give it. Tomorrow, the House among the idols. Day seven hundred.
